title: Citizenship by Descent: What Ghana, Benin and Sierra Leone Ask | Across the Water, Ep. 10
lede: At least 1,213 people have been granted citizenship since 2016 by four West African countries that offer it to descendants of enslaved Africans, according to the Migration Policy Institute. This episode explains how Ghana, Benin, Sierra Leone and Guinea-Bissau differ on price, proof and residence, why Ghana paused applications in February 2026, and what governments hope to gain.
keyPoints: Citizenships granted 2016–26: Ghana 834, Sierra Leone 300, Benin 50, Guinea-Bissau 29; at least 1,213 in total (Migration Policy Institute).

Ghana paused new applications in February 2026 after complaints about cost, stages and a one-week DNA deadline; before the pause it cost US$136 to apply plus US$2,280 for shortlisted applicants (GBC). About 3,000 applied in the 2026 round and 150 were sworn in on March 9 (MPI).

Benin's Law 2024-31 charges a US$100 fee through the My Afro Origins platform; applicants abroad get a three-year provisional status that lapses without residence in Benin (Government of Benin; Globalcit).
Sierra Leone's heritage naturalization route requires a US$100,000 investment and a DNA test, with approval in about 60 days (IMI Daily; MPI).
Ghana's 2019 Year of Return generated US$1.9 billion, according to the Ghana Tourism Authority (MPI).
